Oh absolutely. Today, a can of coke can fit enough microSD cards fit all of the worlds computer storage combined from around 1995. But as the capabilities of our computers grow, so to do our demands on them. I imagine in the next 20 years, we will see the concept of a "screen" projecting a 2d image as archaic in many cases, and instead interact with our devices through some kind of augmented reality interface. which means everyone will be using their devices for 3d rendering calculations in real time, all the time. In 50 to 100 years, I could see neural interfaces becoming the norm, which would likely require the simulation of parts or all of the brain, which will doubtless be taxing. Additionally, there's the matter of optimization; Making your programs run fast is hard, and oftentimes when writing software, developers have to make choices between speed and readability. Oftentimes the solution which is easier to conceptualize (and therefore write), and easier to maintain, is considerably slower than the solution which is most optimal (for an example of this, look up quicksort, one of the most efficient ways to take a list of items, and sort them. Its a pain in the ass to write relative to something like selection sort, but is significantly faster when you get into list sizes of the billions. Incidentally, if you have to sort a list of that size, you've already made a huge mistake efficiency wise, and should probably not have used a list, but lists are easy to conceptualize, so they are a go to datastructure instead of say, a hashset, which would eliminate the need for sorting entirely). In older machines, resources were precious, so code was often optimized to the point of being near illegible to anyone but the author. If one does not have to optimize as aggressively, code is faster to write, at the cost of more resources, plus no one really LIKES spending a ton of time refactoring to save 15 bytes of memory and a few hundred operations... As machines scale up, the resource usage of the software running on them will become less and less efficient for doing the same tasks; It won't really be noticeable to the end user, as the rate at which more resources become available to the system through new hardware releases will outstrip the general reduction in efficiency, but it WILL play a role.

Think about it this way; One tab of chrome takes up more memory today than a dozen firefox windows back in 2000. Sure, chrome has WAY more features as part of that, but part of the reason those features are possible is because less software engineers are stuck trying to improve operation count from log(n) to log(log(n)) on a background task.
